text: I now give the floor to her excellency
Maria Malma Stenagard, Minister of
Foreign Affairs of Sweden.
Mr. President Excellencies, I want to
tell you about my grandmother Alice.
Growing up in rural Sweden, as the
seventh of 11 siblings, her
opportunities were very different from
those of her brothers. Her parents
expected her to focus first and foremost
on family life. Yet, she was curious,
capable, and determined to build a life
of her own. A job at a local bank gave
her not only an income, but also
independence and confidence. There at
the bank, she met many women with little
to no experience with finances and who
were left vulnerable when circumstances
changed.
She wrote in her diary about some of the
women she met, many of whom were
recently widowed, coming to the bank in
tears because they didn't know anything
about their own family finances. One
woman came to the bank holding two safe
deposit keys without knowing which bank
they belonged to.
My grandmother was as independent as a
woman in that time and place could be.
But she worried deeply about the
consequences for the women who were not.
During her life, she witnessed
extraordinary progress. But two
generations later, far too many women
are still entirely economically
dependent on men. Mr. president. 80
years ago when Sweden joined the United
Nations, the foundations of our modern
society were being laid. In the 1940s
and 50s, Swedish women joined the labor
market in large numbers. This was not
only a matter of principle. It also came
from the realization that our econ
economy needed women in the workforce.
Women's economic empowerment is a matter
of freedom. When women work and earn
their own money, their
self-determination grows. Gender
equality is not only the right thing to
do, it's also the smart thing to do.
When women work, economies grow.
Mr. President, each generation must
fight for equality.
the same year my grandmother was born,
Sweden decided that women should have
the right to vote. That very same year,
women in Afghanistan were also granted
the right to vote. More than a century
later, the contrast between women's
freedoms in our two countries is as
striking as it is saddening. It is a
painful reminder that progress is never
irreversible. Rights once gained can be
lost. Freedoms do not defend themselves.
It is up to us to protect them. for
women and girls everywhere and for
generations to come.
Mr. President, when Sweden joined the UN
in 1946, the world was emerging from the
devastation of war. The lesson from that
catastrophe was clear. Peace must not be
taken for granted. Defense of
sovereignty and territorial integrity
has been at the heart of Swedish foreign
policy ever since. Eight decades later,
these principles are once again being
challenged. Bad faith, conflict, and
utter contempt for the common rules are
weakening the institutions that we build
together. These are times of upheaval.
The number of armed conflicts is growing
and civilians are paying the price. In
Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Palestine,
Lebanon, Myanmar, the Democratic
Republic of the Congo, and many other
conflict zones. Millions are suffering.
Mr. President, Russia's aggression
against Ukraine is a blatant violation
of international law. It strikes at the
heart of the very principles upon which
the United Nations was founded. Sweden's
support for Ukraine is felt deeply
throughout our entire society. It comes
from our people, our civil society, and
the business community.
We will support Ukraine for as long as
it takes.
Russia has not only violated the UN
charter, it has repeatedly violated
international humanitarian law and human
rights law. Attacks targeting civilians,
forcible transfer of and deportation of
children, conflict related sexual
violence and torture, the list is far
too long. Ensuring accountability for
these violations is crucial. If there is
anything that we have learned from
history, it is that there cannot be a
just and lasting peace without
accountability.
Sweden stands firmly behind the ICC, its
independence and integrity, and
recognizes its vital role, not least in
Ukraine. Russia must also be held
accountable for its breaches of the
Chemical Weapons Convention, both on and
off the battlefield.
Russia's war of aggression against a
peaceful neighbor is one of the biggest
strategic mistakes and moral failures of
the 21st century.
4 and a half years after launching its
fullscale invasion, Russia has failed to
achieve its objectives. Its economy is
under strain and its casualty numbers
are devastating. Ordinary Russians are
withdrawing their funds from the bank
and a substantial share of Russia's
young people are dying on the front
lines. The impact of Russia's war of
aggression extends far beyond Ukraine.
Russia intensified its systematic
attacks on civilian infrastructure and
on vessels in the Black Sea this summer.
This has once again disrupt disrupted
global food supply chains, exacerbating
an already dire situation for vulnerable
people across the globe.
To President Putin and Mr. Lavrov, I say
this. The path to peace is clear. The
choice should be easy. Withdraw your
troops. end this war.
Mr. President,
Sweden has been an active contributor to
the United Nations for 80 years, and we
remain committed. But as a staunch
partner, we will continue to push for a
UN that is more effective, more
transparent, and better equipped to
uphold the principles of its charter. A
UN that is resolute. Sweden's first
peacekeepers, 300 of them, served this
organization during the Swiss crisis in
1956. Since then, more than 800,000
Swedes have followed in their footsteps.
We have a long tradition of supporting
mediation through the UN. It began in
1948 with UN's first mediator, Sweden's
Falanarot.
We have long been a major donor of
development assistance and we remain
devoted to tackling global development
challenges and contributing to urgent
humanitarian efforts.
Sweden remains a generous donor, but
development assistance alone will not be
enough to meet the challenges before us.
Mr. President, reducing emissions to
curb climate change is a common and
global challenge and is necessary to
safeguard and increase development gains
in the coming decades. Sweden will
continue to promote climate action based
on urgency and opportunity.
Urgency based on what science tells us.
Opportunity based on the economic
growth, jobs, and strengthened
competitiveness that climate transition
brings.
Given the state of the world, changes
are necessary to ensure the UN's central
role in international affairs and its
ability to address today's challenges.
An efficient, effective, nimble, and
well-coordinated UN is urgently needed.
Sweden strongly supports the Secretary
General's UN80 initiative and expects
all UN entities to engage fully with a
clear focus on improving delivery at
country level. We also expect member
states to give the UN adequate
resources. Assessed contributions must
be paid in full and in time.
As members, we also need to carefully
consider institutional reforms and align
mandates with available resources. UN80
is an opportunity to strengthen the UN's
impact across all three pillars and to
reinforce the international system
firmly grounded in the UN Charter of
International Law.
Sweden remains firm in its defense of
the UN's normative mandates on human
rights, gender equality, and sexual and
reproductive health and rights. Everyone
has the right to live freely and with
dignity, to be who they are, and to love
whom they choose. Sweden will always
stand up for that freedom and for equal
rights of all. Mr. President, a balanced
expansion of the Security Council would
strengthen its credibility and the
legitimacy of its decisions. Sweden
would like to see permanent and
non-permanent seats added and a fairer
representation of all continents on the
council.
Africa, home to 1.3 billion people and
the largest regional block in the United
Nations, has no permanent seat. This is
neither logical nor fair. Further, the
veto should never be used to prevent the
UN from acting against serious
violations of international law or in
humanitarian disasters.
Mr. President, we must continue to
strengthen our United Nations to make
the organization stronger and better
equipped to prevent conflict and meet
the challenges of tomorrow. We must
continue to find common agreements based
on the fundamentals, every country's
sovereignty and territorial integrity,
prohibition of the use of force, respect
for international law, human rights and
humanitarian principles.
It is our shared responsibility to
ensure that the UN remains relevant,
effective, and resolute, that it becomes
greater than the sum of its parts
to show once again that we can turn the
page on conflict and chaos and move
towards peace and prosperity.
Mr. President this year also marks 65
years since Secretary General Dog
Hammerald died. His integrity,
conviction, and commitment to the vision
and values of our organization are still
remembered.
Sweden continues to support the UN
investigation aimed at clarifying the
circumstances surrounding Secretary
General Hamahul's death.
And I would like to conclude with the
words of Mr. Hammer.
It is no news to anybody, but we sense
it in different degrees that the world
of today is more than ever before one
world. The weakness of one is the
weakness of all. And the strength of
one, not the military strength, the real
strength, the economic and social
strength, the happiness of the people is
indirectly the strength of all. Thank
you.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs
of Sweden.
